extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and patent litigators (users of model jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials describing jury questions and legal standards for claim construction, various theories of infringement, and defenses (including invalidity). Intended to guide judges in instructing juries and attorneys in preparing/verifying jury instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict Questions — Damages and Other Patent Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: What amount of damages, if any, [the Plaintiff] has proven. [LIST ANY OTHER PATENT ISSUES]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Verdict Form contains specific questions (including damages and other patent issues) that jurors will answer. Tailor and list additional patent issues as needed on the verdict form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you decide whether [the Defendant] has infringed the claims of [the Plaintiff]’s patent or whether [the Plaintiff]’s patent is invalid, you will have to understand the patent claims. The patent claims are numbered sentences at the end of the patent. ... The claims are intended to define, in words, the boundaries of the inventor’s rights. Only the claims of the patent can be infringed. Neither the written description, nor the drawings of a patent can be infringed. Each of the claims must be considered individually. You must use the same claim meaning for both your decision on infringement and your decision on invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 35 U.S.C. § 112 and Federal Circuit/SCOTUS precedent (Phillips, Markman, Catalina Lighting). Emphasize that only claims define what can be infringed and that the same constructions apply for infringement and invalidity determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction for the Case
rubrics_metrics.description: It is my job as judge to provide to you the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted. You must accept the meanings I give you and use them when you decide whether any claim has been infringed and whether any claim is invalid. I will now tell you the meanings of the following words and groups of words from the patent claims. [READ STIPULATIONS AND COURT’S CLAIM CONSTRUCTIONS]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge provides constructions (including stipulated constructions). Jurors must accept the court's constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Means-Plus-Function Claims for the Case
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may express an element for a claim in the form of a “means” or “step” for performing a function. ... This clause requires special interpretation. This element does not cover all [[means] [steps]] that perform the recited function of “___________________________.” Rather, I have determined that the recited function is “_____________________.” I have determined that the corresponding [[structure] [step]] described in the patent specification and drawings that perform this recited function is “_______________________________,” or an equivalent of this corresponding [[structure] or [step]]. You must use this interpretation ... in your deliberations regarding infringement and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give Instruction 2.2 only if the case involves means-plus-function claims. Include construction of limitations governed by 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6 (or §112(f)). Consider whether Instruction 2.2 is unnecessary where the limitation does not use “means for” or “step for.” Relevant cases cited (Mettler-Toledo; JVW; Utah Med.; Valmont).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: I will now instruct you as to the rules you must follow when deciding whether [the Plaintiff] has proven that [the Defendant] infringed any of the claims of the [abbreviated patent number] patent. Patent law gives the owner of a valid patent the right to exclude others from importing, making, using, offering to sell, or selling [[the claimed invention] [a product made by a method claimed in the patent]] within the United States during the term of the patent. ... in deciding the issue of infringement you may not compare [the Defendant]’s accused [[product] [method]] to [the Plaintiff]’s commercial [[product] [method]]. Rather, ... you must compare the [Defendant]’s accused [[product] [method]] to the claims of the [abbreviated patent number] patent. A claim of a patent may be infringed directly or indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish direct v indirect infringement, literal v doctrine of equivalents, and induced v contributory infringement. Practice note: avoid jury confusion by distinguishing these theories clearly and separating direct vs indirect and literal vs equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Knowledge of the Patent and Intent to Infringe Are Immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] is liable for directly infringing [the Plaintiff]’s patent if you find that [the Plaintiff] has proven that it is more likely than not that [the Defendant] made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention defined in at least one claim of [the Plaintiff]’s patent during the term of the patent. A party can directly infringe a patent without knowing of the patent or without knowing that what the party is doing is patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard: preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Cite 35 U.S.C. § 271(a) and supporting case law (Commil; Medtronic; Global-Tech; Warner-Jenkinson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Literal Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine literal infringement, you must compare the accused [[product] [method]] with each patent claim [the Plaintiff] asserts is infringed. A patent claim is literally infringed only if [the Defendant]’s [[product] [method]] includes each and every [[element] [method step]] recited in that patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine literal infringement separately for each asserted claim. If accused product lacks one or more elements, there is no literal infringement. Cite case law (Limelight; Hutchins; Gen. Mills; Amstar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Joint Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: You may find that [the Defendant] directly infringes if you find (1) that [the Defendant] personally performed all acts necessary to infringe, or (2) that the steps performed by [the other party] are attributable to [the Defendant]. You may find that the steps are attributable to [the Defendant] if you find that either (a) [the Defendant] exercised direction or control over [the other party] when the other party performed these acts or (b) [the Defendant] and [the other party] formed a joint enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting joint infringement via joint enterprise, prove four elements: agreement, common purpose, community of pecuniary interest, and equal right of control. Practice note: where both joint infringement and inducement are alleged, consider instructing back-to-back to highlight differences and required evidence. Cite Limelight; Eli Lilly v. Teva; Akamai; Nalco.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal Infringement of Means-Plus-Function or Step-Plus-Function Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement, [the Plaintiff] must prove that it is more likely than not that the [[part of the Defendant’s product] [step in the Defendant’s method]] (1) performs the recited function of “________________________________________________________,” and (2) is identical or equivalent to the [[structure] [step]] described in the patent specification and drawings for performing this recited function, namely, “____________________________.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First decide whether accused product has any structure performing the recited function; next decide whether that structure is the same as or equivalent to the structure recited in the specification. Equivalence may be shown by insubstantial differences or performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result (person of ordinary skill perspective). Cite 35 U.S.C. §112 and relevant case law (Williamson; Gen. Protecht; Applied Med.; A1-Site; Chiuminatta; Cybor; In re Donaldson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of Dependent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim in the patent. A dependent claim includes all elements recited in the dependent claim, as well as all elements of the independent claim to which it refers. To establish literal infringement of [Dependent Claim], [the Plaintiff] must show that it is more likely than not that [the Defendant]’s [[product] [method]] includes each and every element of [Independent Claim] and [Dependent Claim]. If you find that [Independent Claim] from which [Dependent Claim] depends is not literally infringed, then you must find that [Dependent Claim] is also not literally infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain independent v dependent claims with examples. Cite Wahpeton Canvas; Shatterproof Glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of “Comprising,” “Consisting of,” and “Consisting Essentially of” Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: (Alternative 1: “comprising”) The word “comprising” means “including the following but not excluding others.” ... (Alternative 2: “consisting of”) The word “consisting of” means “including the following and excluding others.” ... (Alternative 3: “consisting essentially of”) means “including the following and possibly including unlisted [[components] [method steps]] that do not materially affect the invention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how additional components/method steps affect literal infringement depending on claim open/closed language. Cite Shire Dev.; Multilayer Stretch; other Federal Circuit cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Doctrine of Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: If you decide that [the Defendant]’s [[product] [method]] does not literally infringe an asserted patent claim, you must then decide whether it is more likely than not that the [[product] [method]] infringes the asserted claim under the doctrine of equivalents. Under the doctrine of equivalents, the [[product] [method]] can infringe ... if it includes [[components] [method steps]] that are equivalent to those elements of the claim that are not literally present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each missing element individually for equivalence. Equivalence can be shown by insubstantial differences or performing substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. Consider whether persons of ordinary skill would have known interchangeability at time of infringement; known interchangeability is not necessary. Note: same accused component may satisfy multiple claim elements, or two components may satisfy a single claim element. Cite Warner-Jenkinson; Graver Tank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on the Doctrine of Equivalents—Prosecution History Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history estoppel: if the patentee made a representation or argument, or amended a claim for reasons related to patentability, the presumption that equivalent subject matter has been surrendered may apply. I have determined, as a matter of law, that the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to certain elements of the asserted claims: [LIST ELEMENTS]. Consequently each of the elements above must be literally present within [the Defendant]’s [[product] [method]] for there to be infringement of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction given only if the Court has determined prosecution history estoppel applies as a matter of law. Explain presumption and how it can be rebutted (Festo). Cite Festo; Warner-Jenkinson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on the Doctrine of Equivalents—Subject Matter Dedicated to the Public
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Court has determined that certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to the listed elements. Consequently each of the elements above must be literally present for there to be infringement of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give only where court has determined dedication applies as a matter of law. Cite SanDisk; Pfizer; PSC Computer Prods.; Toro; Johnson & Johnston.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively Inducing Patent Infringement (Inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that [the Defendant] actively induced infringement, [the Plaintiff] must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (A) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement ... and (B) [the Defendant] actively induced these acts of infringement by [alleged direct infringer]. To prove active inducement, [the Plaintiff] must establish that it is more likely than not that: (1) [the Defendant] aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with the intent to cause acts ... that would constitute direct infringement; (2) [the Defendant] knew of the patent, or showed willful blindness to the existence of the patent, at that time; (3) [the Defendant] knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the [alleged direct infringer] would infringe at least one claim of the patent; and (4) [alleged direct infringer] infringed at least one patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove all four elements. Define willful blindness: subjective belief of high probability a patent existed and deliberate actions to avoid learning of the patent. Cite 35 U.S.C. §271(b) and cases (Commil; Limelight; Global-Tech; Takeda; Info-Hold; DSU; Metabolite; Ferguson; Hewlett-Packard). Practice note: clarify difference between joint infringement and inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supply of All or a Substantial Portion of the Components to Another Country (§271(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: [Plaintiff] asserts that [Defendant] infringed by supplying all or a substantial portion of the components of the patented product from the United States to another country and actively inducing the assembly of those components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the United States. To show infringement under §271(f)(1), [Plaintiff] must prove more likely than not: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one claim; (2) [Defendant] supplied components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention; and (3) [Defendant] specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into an infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'substantial portion' requires a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment—the export of a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability. Practice note: §271(f)(1) does not apply to method claims. Cite 35 U.S.C. §271(f)(1); Life Techs.; Cardiac Pacemakers; Microsoft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory Infringement (§271(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: To find contributory infringement, Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) someone other than [Defendant] has directly infringed a claim; (2) [Defendant] sold, offered for sale, or imported within the U.S. a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing method; (3) the component or apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (4) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the claimed invention; and (5) [Defendant] knew that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing [[product] [method]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'staple article capable of substantial non-infringing use' (uses other than as part of patented product that are not occasional/farfetched/impractical). Defendant's knowledge may be shown by willful blindness (subjective belief of high probability and deliberate actions to avoid learning of patent). Cite 35 U.S.C. §271(c) and cases (Commil; Global-Tech; Aro; Toshiba; R+L Carriers; Spansion; Fujitsu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supply of Components Especially Made or Adapted (§271(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff asserts that Defendant infringed by supplying components of a claimed invention from the U.S. into a foreign country where the exported components were especially made or adapted for use in an invention covered by the patent and have no substantial non-infringing uses, and where Defendant knew the components were especially made or adapted and intended for the components to be combined in a way that would have infringed the patent if combined in the U.S. To show infringement under §271(f)(2) Plaintiff must prove: (1) Defendant actually supplied the components from the U.S. into a foreign country; (2) Defendant knew or should have known components were especially made/adapted for use in an infringing product; (3) components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) Defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually were combined abroad; intent to combine into an infringing product suffices. Cite 35 U.S.C. §271(f)(2); WesternGeco; Microsoft; Cardiac Pacemakers; Waymark; Rotec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Import, Sale, Offer for Sale or Use of Product Made by Patented Process (§271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff asserts Defendant infringed by [[importing] [selling] [offering for sale] [using]] a product that was made by a process covered by one or more claims of the patent. To show infringement under §271(g), Plaintiff must prove: (1) Defendant imported/sold/offered/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim; (2) the product was made between [issue date] and [expiration/trial date]; and (3) Defendant imported/sold/offered/used the product between [issue date] and [expiration/trial date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether evidence shows the product was 'made by' the claimed process. If product was materially changed by later processes or is only a trivial/non-essential part of another product, then it was not 'made by' the claimed process. Infringement under §271(g) does not require a single entity to perform the patented process. Cite 35 U.S.C. §271(g); Syngenta; Amgen; NTP; Mycogen; Biotec; Eli Lilly; Bio-Technology Gen. Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of Invalidity Defense (Burden and Contentions)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that the asserted claim(s) of the patent[s]-in-suit are invalid. [The Defendant] must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid. Claims of an issued patent may be found to be invalid. Thus, you must determine whether each of [the Plaintiff]’s claims is invalid. [The Defendant] contends that patent claims [insert claim numbers] are invalid for the following reasons: [Insert invalidity contentions]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will instruct in more detail on invalidity grounds. Note the heightened burden (clear and convincing) for proving invalidity of issued patent claims. Include specific invalidity contentions on the instruction/verdict form.
